Um so, I'm curious if if you could explain to us what was broken about the

Uh this wasn't like original research from
us. The idea of a super BP tokenizer was published by a group at the University
of Washington. Basically, a a tokenizer is what breaks
up language into individual chunks that your AI model sees.
And typically, the way people build tokenizers is they always split at white
space. So, it's it has a word boundary. This group, what they observed was like
why are we doing that? Some words don't really deserve to be
modeled individually cuz they're just so frequently before another word or
something. What happens if you only have that constraint? It turns out you get
21% less uh token outputs for a given prompt.
And this is one of those things that it it just made sense for us cuz we're
trying to build a fastest VLM. Uh 20% win with no downsides, no loss in sense.
I think the reason a lot of people don't pursue this is it's it's not seen as

it's medium effort, I would say. There's Like it's it's not rocket

an engineering shop. I

specific improvements that you made um um sort of with this lens in mind?
>> Yeah, um we So so we recently built released a new custom inference engine
specifically for Hungry because we realized that the existing inference
engines don't really get towards LLM inference and VLMs have like different

Uh and we've gone deep into the woods optimizing this. We wanted to make it
work for pretty much any inference hardware that people wanted to run on
anywhere from like cheap foreign devices, sometimes even
CPUs to high-end server chips like Blackwells.
Uh we got to a point where like our kernels weren't even the bottlenecks
anymore. Like it was image decoding >> Mhm.
>> was slowing us down. So then we had to like sit down and write custom image
decoding, image resizing uh libraries and native code to
to tackle that part of the bottleneck. But yeah, it's really whatever is the

>> So um I want to talk about hallucination a bit because um hallucination in vision
models feels like it's a real problem, but it doesn't get much attention
compared to uh how often we talk about hallucination in in text-based models.
What does video hallucination actually look like in the wild and how do you
think about it from a model design standpoint?
>> That's a really good question. Hallucinations are one of the
big things preventing customers from like really taking advantage of AI in
the vision space in the wild.
If you can't really trust your system and you don't understand how it's making
decisions, what its failure modes are, it's really hard to trust it when you're
deploying it in production. Our approach to this has really been to
focus on grounding. So, when Moonbeam answers a question
we we built a reasoning mode where we require that like if you ask it like
is is this car parked within the lines or is it slightly
outside as a random example. Um rather than directly answering yes or
no, the model actually goes behind the scenes and says, I see a car here, these
are its boundaries, I see the lines here. It'll actually give you like
grounded XY coordinates. Um in in the reasoning uh in the
reasoning phase that you can track down. >> Mhm.
>> So, that allows us to inspect as a model like
as a as a person trying to get the model to task what the failure modes are.
And where there are failure modes, it it tells you what you need to correct. Um
so, we do that. That has helped us a lot.
We we also do ex- we spend extensive compute on reinforcement learning on
these grounding-related reasoning chains.
We we train on over 200 tasks at this point where it it
really forces the model to be very accurate in in generating these
grounding decisions. And so, that's been our general
approach. It it helps our customers because they can understand why the
model made a decision, so there's some explainability built into it.
And it helps us as model developers
understand where hallucinations happen, how to recommend
